tamsulosin.name: Tamsulosin
tamsulosin.summary: Tamsulosin is an alpha blocker prescribed mainly for the urinary difficulties caused by an enlarged prostate gland. It relaxes the muscle around the bladder and prostate so that peeing becomes easier. Dizziness on standing is a known effect, and the NHS asks people to tell the doctor about it before cataract or glaucoma surgery.
usedFor: Difficulty peeing caused by an enlarged prostate gland
Lower urinary tract symptoms linked to benign prostatic hyperplasia, such as poor stream, dribbling and passing urine often (described in the emc patient leaflet)
Occasionally, helping kidney stones pass through the urinary tract
tamsulosin.howItWorks: Tamsulosin belongs to the group of medicines called alpha blockers (alpha-adrenoreceptor antagonists). In an enlarged prostate it relaxes the muscle around the bladder and the prostate gland, which makes it easier to pee. The NHS says it is sometimes also used to ease the passing of kidney stones.
tamsulosin.onset: The NHS says tamsulosin works best when it is taken over a long time, rather than acting as a short-term fix.

common: The NHS says most people have no side effects or only minor ones that often ease as the body adjusts.
Dizziness, especially on sitting or standing, and ejaculation problems (such as little or no semen) are the main common side effects.
When dizziness, light-headedness or sweating occurs, the NHS says sitting or lying down until it passes helps, and alcohol, driving, cycling and using tools or machinery are best avoided meanwhile.
serious: Fainting is listed by the NHS as a rare serious effect; for serious side effects the NHS says to call NHS 111.

A prolonged, painful erection (priapism) is listed by the NHS as a rare serious effect and is described in the emc leaflet as a very rare effect that is usually unrelated to sexual activity; the NHS route for serious side effects is NHS 111.
A serious allergic reaction (anaphylaxis) is rare and can cause a swollen throat or tongue, a raised itchy rash or difficulty breathing; the NHS says this needs a 999 call.

cautions: The NHS says most adults can take tamsulosin, but it is not suitable for everyone.
It is not suitable for people who have had an allergic reaction to tamsulosin or similar medicines such as alfuzosin, doxazosin, prazosin or terazosin.

Those with orthostatic hypotension (low blood pressure that causes dizziness on standing), severe liver or kidney problems, or a history of fainting while or just after peeing are also listed as people who should not take it.

People due to have cataract or glaucoma surgery are asked to tell the doctor in advance that they take tamsulosin, because it may cause complications during the operation; the doctor may advise stopping beforehand.
Intraoperative floppy iris syndrome, a problem with the pupil widening during cataract surgery, has been associated with tamsulosin in emc patient leaflets.
Other alpha blockers and medicines for high blood pressure can lower blood pressure too much when taken with tamsulosin.
The NHS advises against taking it with diclofenac, and says paracetamol, codeine and NSAIDs such as ibuprofen are fine.
Alcohol is best avoided in the first few days, until it is clear how the medicine affects a person, because it can increase the risk of side effects.
Tamsulosin is not usually used in pregnancy or breastfeeding, according to the NHS.
tamsulosin.monitoring: NICE guidance on lower urinary tract symptoms in men recommends reviewing symptoms, quality of life and side effects after starting an alpha blocker and then at regular intervals.

sections.heading: What is tamsulosin used for?
sections.body: Tamsulosin is a medicine that the NHS describes as a treatment for an enlarged prostate. It is mainly prescribed for difficulty peeing that the enlarged prostate gland causes. The emc patient leaflet describes use for lower urinary tract complaints linked to benign prostatic hyperplasia, including a poor stream, dribbling and needing to pass urine often. The NHS also says tamsulosin is sometimes used to help kidney stones pass through the urinary tract. NICE guidance for men with moderate to severe symptoms lists alfuzosin, doxazosin, tamsulosin and terazosin as alpha blocker options. Drug treatment is offered when other management options have been unsuccessful or are not appropriate, the guideline says. The medicine comes as prolonged-release capsules and tablets, and the NHS lists several brand names, including Contiflo XL, Flomaxtra XL and Tabphyn MR. A combined product containing tamsulosin and solifenacin is sold as Vesomni, and one with dutasteride as Combodart.

sections.heading: How does tamsulosin work?
sections.body: Tamsulosin is classed as an alpha blocker, also called an alpha-adrenoreceptor antagonist. In a man with an enlarged prostate, it relaxes the muscle around the bladder and prostate gland. With that muscle more relaxed, peeing becomes easier. In some cases the same effect is used to ease the passing of kidney stones. Because alpha blockers relax muscle, they can also lower blood pressure, which is why dizziness is a recognised effect. The NHS says tamsulosin works best when taken for a long time, and that for an enlarged prostate it can be continued long term if it is helping. Stopping suddenly could let symptoms come back, so the NHS says to talk to a doctor before stopping. The medicine is swallowed whole with a drink of water, and is not broken, chewed or crushed.

sections.heading: Side effects
sections.body: The NHS says most people have no side effects, or only mild ones that often ease as the body adjusts. The main common effects are dizziness, particularly on sitting or standing, and ejaculation problems, which can mean little or no semen. If dizziness, light-headedness or sweating starts, the NHS says sitting or lying down until it passes helps. Alcohol, driving, cycling and using tools or machinery are best avoided at that time. The NHS lists fainting and priapism, a painful erection that does not go away, among rare serious effects. The emc leaflet calls a persistent painful erection unrelated to sexual activity very rare. For serious side effects the NHS says to call NHS 111. A serious allergic reaction (anaphylaxis) is also rare, and can bring a swollen throat or tongue, a raised itchy rash or difficulty breathing, which the NHS treats as a 999 emergency. If side effects are bothersome, the NHS says a doctor may be able to offer a different medicine.

sections.heading: Eye surgery and who needs extra care
sections.body: The NHS says most adults can take tamsulosin, though it is not suitable for everyone. People who have had an allergic reaction to it or to similar alpha blockers are listed as unsuitable. So are those with orthostatic hypotension, which is low blood pressure that causes dizziness or light-headedness on standing. Severe liver or kidney problems, and a history of fainting while peeing or just afterwards, are also on the NHS list. Another point concerns the eyes: tamsulosin may cause complications during cataract or glaucoma surgery. Intraoperative floppy iris syndrome, in which the pupil dilates poorly during cataract surgery, has been linked to tamsulosin in emc leaflets. The NHS says a person due to have this surgery tells the doctor about tamsulosin in advance, and the doctor may advise stopping it beforehand. The NHS says tamsulosin is not usually used in pregnancy or breastfeeding.

sections.heading: Other medicines and alcohol
sections.body: Other alpha blockers, such as doxazosin, alfuzosin, prazosin or terazosin, may lower blood pressure when combined with tamsulosin. Medicines for high blood pressure can also lower it too much when taken alongside it. The NHS advises against combining tamsulosin with diclofenac. It describes paracetamol, codeine and NSAIDs such as ibuprofen as fine to take with it. Alcohol is best avoided during the first few days, until it is clear how the medicine affects a person. The NHS notes that alcohol can increase the risk of side effects. Herbal remedies and supplements are covered on a separate NHS page, and a pharmacist or doctor can check any new product against tamsulosin.

faqs.q: Is tamsulosin used for anything other than an enlarged prostate?
faqs.a: The NHS says it is mainly prescribed for difficulty peeing caused by an enlarged prostate. It is also sometimes used to help kidney stones pass, and the NHS mentions prostatitis as an occasional use.

faqs.q: Can tamsulosin be taken for a long time?
faqs.a: The NHS says tamsulosin is generally taken long term for an enlarged prostate if it is helping. It also says the medicine works best when taken over a long time.

faqs.q: What happens if tamsulosin is stopped suddenly?
faqs.a: The NHS says stopping suddenly could make symptoms come back. A doctor is the person to talk to about stopping or changing treatment.

The NHS says tamsulosin may cause complications during cataract or glaucoma surgery. A person due for this surgery tells the doctor about the medicine in advance, and the doctor may advise stopping it beforehand.

faqs.q: Which side effects need urgent help?
faqs.a: Fainting, a painful erection that does not go away and other serious side effects are routed to NHS 111 by the NHS. Signs of a serious allergic reaction, such as a swollen throat or tongue or difficulty breathing, are a 999 emergency.

alpha-blockers.name: Alpha blockers
alpha-blockers.summary: Alpha blockers, also called alpha-adrenoreceptor antagonists, are medicines that relax muscle; tamsulosin is used to relax the muscle around the bladder and prostate in an enlarged prostate.
alpha-blockers.mechanism: In an enlarged prostate, tamsulosin relaxes the muscle around the bladder and prostate gland, which makes it easier to pee.
cautions: Taking more than one alpha blocker, or combining one with medicines for high blood pressure, can lower blood pressure too much.
Orthostatic hypotension, low blood pressure causing dizziness on standing, is listed by the NHS as a reason tamsulosin is not suitable.
classEffects: Dizziness or light-headedness, especially on standing.
An allergic reaction to one alpha blocker, such as alfuzosin, doxazosin, prazosin or terazosin, is a reason the NHS lists against tamsulosin.
